title: Step Brothers
full_review:
"Step Brothers" (Columbia/Relativity) is a confrontational comedy that takes the Peter Pan syndrome to frantic extremes.

As they breathlessly prepare to consummate their experience of love at first sight, and hurriedly introduce themselves, Dr. Robert Doback (Richard Jenkins) and his girlfriend of a few minutes, Nancy Huff (Mary Steenburgen), discover that they're both victims of this social trend, since each has a middle-age but immature stay-at-home son from a previous marriage.

To the extent that the two slackers in question display any ambition at all, Dale Doback (John C. Reilly) is a vaguely aspiring drummer, while Brennan Huff (Will Ferrell) is a would-be singer with terminal stage fright. Both spend their days pursuing the lazy lifestyle of pampered high school students on summer vacation.

Once their parents marry and they're living under the same roof, though, they concentrate on rivaling each other for negative attention and annoying one another with elaborate -- sometimes obscene -- pranks. Their conflict climaxes violently in a front-lawn free-for-all that only ends when they simultaneously knock each other unconscious.

With the newlyweds on the point of despair, a visit from Brennan's smarmily successful younger brother, Derek (Adam Scott), causes the pair to refocus their enmity. After getting a taste of Derek's mocking disdain, Dale punches him in the face and wins Brennan's admiration.

As the stepbrothers bond, and Derek's put-upon wife, Alice (Kathryn Hahn), shows her appreciation for Dale's fighting prowess by making aggressive sexual advances, it becomes apparent that the legal siblings are even more destructive in tandem.

Ferrell's pouting disappointment with the world and Reilly's snarling truculence make for some funny interludes, while nasty but charismatic Scott is a fascinating comic nightmare. Yet director and co-writer (with Ferrell) Adam McKay's film follows a recipe by now closely associated with Judd Apatow -- who serves here only as producer -- one that mixes the moral with the outrageous.

In this case, there are affirmations of familial loyalty and reconciliation, and a positive message about balancing maturity with enduring idealism. But the determination to shock leads the script awry into all manner of distasteful excess.

The film contains nongraphic premarital and adulterous sexual activity, frontal male nudity, pervasive sexual and scatological humor, drug and pornography references, pervasive rough and crude language and some profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
